buildings.name: Taj Mahal
buildings.summary: A marble mausoleum whose central dome, four minarets and formal garden create a carefully ordered riverfront ensemble.
buildings.history: Shah Jahan commissioned the mausoleum for Mumtaz Mahal beside the Yamuna. UNESCO distinguishes the main tomb’s completion in 1648 from later ancillary works completed in 1653; its descriptions also use different starting years, so this record retains that uncertainty.
buildings.layout_notes: The tomb stands on a raised terrace beyond a formally divided garden. Four minarets frame the central domed building, while subsidiary structures and a monumental entrance organize the approach.

buildings.name: Agra Fort
buildings.summary: A fortified imperial precinct containing successive palaces, audience halls and courts above the Yamuna.
buildings.history: The Mughal imperial fortress preserves buildings from several reigns rather than one construction campaign. Its sandstone enclosure contains palace buildings, audience halls and mosques, illustrating changes in courtly requirements and architectural treatment.
buildings.layout_notes: Fortified gates lead into successive courts and palace precincts. The Jahangiri Mahal, Khas Mahal and audience halls should be read as distinct components within the larger enclosure.

buildings.name: Fatehpur Sikri
buildings.summary: Akbar’s former capital brings ceremonial courts, columned pavilions and religious buildings into a planned sandstone city.
buildings.history: Akbar established a planned imperial capital here in the 1570s. Administrative, residential and religious buildings were arranged around courts; the court moved to Lahore in 1585, but the surviving city retains its ceremonial organization.
buildings.layout_notes: The complex includes palaces, public audience spaces, columned pavilions and a mosque precinct. Levels and courtyards separate public circulation from more restricted royal spaces.

buildings.name: Qutb Minar
buildings.summary: A tapering masonry minaret articulated by fluting, projecting balconies and carved inscription bands.
buildings.history: The minaret forms part of a larger early Sultanate ensemble at Mehrauli. Successive construction and repair phases shaped the tower now visible; nearby mosques, tombs and gateways belong to the complex but are not interchangeable with the minaret itself.
buildings.layout_notes: The circular tower narrows upward through successive storeys. Alternating fluted surfaces, inscription bands and projecting balconies articulate the elevation.
buildings.date_label: Late 12th century onward; successive storeys and repairs

buildings.name: Humayun’s Tomb
buildings.summary: A monumental garden tomb combining a raised platform, symmetrical arched elevations and a double dome.
buildings.history: The monument is a major early Mughal garden tomb, dated by UNESCO to 1570. Its raised composition, symmetrical garden and dressed-stone structure clad in sandstone and marble form a carefully integrated funerary landscape.
buildings.layout_notes: Paths and water channels divide the garden around the elevated tomb. Repeated arched openings and the central double dome establish the building’s symmetrical external composition.
buildings.date_label: Circa 1570 CE; construction range varies by account

buildings.name: Red Fort
buildings.summary: Shah Jahan’s palace-fort organizes pavilions and ceremonial spaces within an imposing red sandstone enclosure.
buildings.history: Shah Jahan built the palace-fort for his new capital, Shahjahanabad. Its private pavilions were connected by the Nahr-i-Behisht water channel; later interventions mean the surviving complex should not be treated as an unchanged seventeenth-century plan.
buildings.layout_notes: Strong enclosure walls and monumental entrances frame more delicate courts and pavilions. Public ceremonial spaces and private apartments form different sequences within the palace precinct.

buildings.name: Great Stupa at Sanchi
buildings.summary: A hemispherical Buddhist reliquary mound encircled by a stone railing and richly carved directional gateways.
buildings.history: The Great Stupa developed from an early Buddhist foundation through later enlargement and the addition of stone railings and carved gateways. The wider Sanchi complex includes monuments from many centuries; this record’s broad range describes principal early phases of Stupa 1.
buildings.layout_notes: A hemispherical mound encloses the reliquary core. Circumambulatory routes, railings and four directional toranas structure ritual movement and offer surfaces for narrative carving.
buildings.date_label: 3rd century BCE core; enlargements and gateways followed

buildings.name: Kandariya Mahadeva Temple
buildings.summary: A Chandella temple whose clustered towers rise above an elevated platform and densely carved wall surfaces.
buildings.history: The temple belongs to the Chandella architectural flowering at Khajuraho. Its sculptural program is integral to the architecture, while the clustered sanctuary towers create a rising composition rather than a single isolated vertical mass.
buildings.layout_notes: An elevated platform supports a sequence of halls leading toward the sanctuary. Curved towers and smaller associated spires emphasize the inner sacred space.

buildings.name: Ajanta Cave 1
buildings.summary: A rock-cut Buddhist monastery with a pillared hall, shrine and celebrated painted interiors.
buildings.history: Cave 1 belongs to Ajanta’s later Buddhist phase, distinct from the earlier caves of the group. Its paintings and sculpture combine a devotional setting with a monastic interior; the source dates the wider later group to the fifth and sixth centuries.
buildings.layout_notes: A verandah leads into a pillared hall and a rear shrine. Painted wall surfaces and sculpted supports are architectural evidence that should be examined separately from the cave’s broader historical date.
buildings.date_label: 5th–6th-century later Ajanta phase; Cave 1 attribution approximate

buildings.name: Kailasa Temple, Ellora
buildings.summary: A freestanding-looking temple excavated from living rock, with a deep court, sculpted walls and subsidiary structures.
buildings.history: Kailasa is the major monolithic Hindu temple within Ellora’s multi-religious cave complex. Excavation removed surrounding basalt to create courts, built-looking forms and sculptural surfaces from the parent rock.
buildings.layout_notes: A deep open court surrounds the main temple mass. Gateways, subsidiary spaces and relief-covered walls create a sequence that differs from a cave simply cut into a cliff face.

buildings.name: Elephanta Cave 1
buildings.summary: A columned Shaiva cave sanctuary with monumental relief panels arranged around a rock-cut sacred interior.
buildings.history: UNESCO dates the principal Shaiva cave architecture to approximately the mid-fifth to sixth centuries. The great Cave 1 combines a square columned interior with monumental reliefs, including the celebrated three-headed form of Shiva.
buildings.layout_notes: Rows of columns organize the main hall; porticos open on multiple sides. The shrine and sculptural panels establish distinct focal points within the excavated interior.

buildings.name: Sun Temple, Konark
buildings.summary: A temple conceived as Surya’s monumental chariot, distinguished by carved wheels and extensive architectural sculpture.
buildings.history: The temple expresses the solar deity Surya’s chariot through architectural scale, carved wheels and sculptural programs. The thirteenth-century ensemble survives incompletely, so remaining halls and sculptures should not be mistaken for the original complete temple.
buildings.layout_notes: Carved chariot wheels articulate the raised base. Monumental surviving masses, subsidiary remains and sculptural bands reveal the original ceremonial composition.
buildings.date_label: 13th century CE; reign of Narasimhadeva I

buildings.name: Brihadisvara Temple
buildings.summary: Rajaraja I’s monumental temple places a tall pyramidal sanctuary tower within a large enclosed precinct.
buildings.history: The temple is associated with Rajaraja I and the early eleventh-century Chola state. It remains part of a living religious tradition; painting, sculpture and stone construction complement the monumental sanctuary tower.
buildings.layout_notes: The tall pyramidal vimana dominates a broad enclosed court. Gateways and subsidiary structures establish an axial approach to the sanctuary.

buildings.name: Airavatesvara Temple
buildings.summary: A compact Chola temple whose sculpted halls and chariot-like forms reward close study of its stonework.
buildings.history: Built under Rajaraja II, the twelfth-century temple is one of UNESCO’s Great Living Chola Temples. Its smaller scale compared with Thanjavur allows attention to the refinement of its sculpture and hall architecture.
buildings.layout_notes: The sanctuary tower and richly articulated mandapa form the main composition. Chariot-like sculptural treatment and finely worked supports distinguish its ceremonial spaces.
buildings.date_label: 12th century CE; reign of Rajaraja II

buildings.name: Shore Temple
buildings.summary: A coastal structural-temple ensemble with tiered towers and an enclosure of sculpted Nandi figures.
buildings.history: The Shore Temple belongs to the Pallava architectural landscape at Mahabalipuram. Unlike the group’s rock-cut caves and monolithic rathas, it represents structural temple building beside the sea.
buildings.layout_notes: Two prominent tiered towers and associated shrines occupy a compact coastal precinct. Nandi figures along the enclosure reinforce the shrine ensemble’s sculptural setting.

buildings.name: Meenakshi Sundareswarar Temple
buildings.summary: A living temple complex organized around twin sanctuaries, monumental gateway towers, courts and pillared halls.
buildings.history: The Madurai complex developed around the shrines of Meenakshi and Sundareswarar and preserves important Nayak-period work. The district account emphasizes its sculptured pillars, paintings and musical stone supports; the building history cannot be reduced to one founding year.
buildings.layout_notes: Nested precincts and gateway towers surround the twin shrines. The Thousand Pillar Hall and processional corridors provide distinct architectural experiences within the living temple.

buildings.name: Rani-ki-Vav
buildings.summary: A deeply descending stepwell whose pillared levels and sculpted walls turn water infrastructure into a ceremonial architectural space.
buildings.history: The eleventh-century stepwell was conceived as a memorial and as a carefully designed water structure. UNESCO interprets it as an inverted temple, with multiple descending levels and extensive religious, mythological and secular sculpture.
buildings.layout_notes: Stair flights descend through pillared levels toward the well. Sculptural panels line the walls, connecting structural rhythm, water access and ceremonial movement.

buildings.name: Sun Temple, Modhera
buildings.summary: A solar-temple ensemble connecting a stepped reservoir, a richly carved assembly hall and the main shrine.
buildings.history: Gujarat Tourism, citing ASI, places construction in 1026–1027 under Bhima I. The ensemble combines solar devotion with a highly articulated reservoir and halls, rather than presenting only an isolated sanctuary.
buildings.layout_notes: The Suryakund reservoir precedes the Sabha Mandap. Steps and subsidiary shrines frame the water, while carved pillars mediate the approach toward the main shrine.

buildings.name: Amber Fort
buildings.summary: A hilltop palace-fort with successive courts, gateways and ceremonial halls overlooking the Maota Lake.
buildings.history: The palace-fort developed through successive Kachwaha building campaigns, beginning under Man Singh I in 1592. Its external defensive character contrasts with decorated interiors and ceremonial halls in sandstone and marble.
buildings.layout_notes: Monumental gates enter the Jaleb Chowk and subsequent palace courts. Public and private halls, mirrored spaces and views toward Maota Lake structure the visitor’s movement.

buildings.name: Hawa Mahal
buildings.summary: A tall street-facing palace screen whose many small projecting windows create a distinctive honeycomb elevation.
buildings.history: Sawai Pratap Singh commissioned the palace façade in 1799. Its characteristic screened windows form part of Jaipur’s historic urban architecture and allowed views of street activity from within the palace.
buildings.layout_notes: A vertically layered street elevation is articulated by many small projecting windows. The façade’s light and air-filtering openings are its primary architectural focus.

buildings.name: Jaisalmer Fort
buildings.summary: A living fortified settlement of golden-coloured stone, with gates, bastions, palaces and religious buildings.
buildings.history: The fort is a long-lived urban enclosure rather than a single palace. UNESCO’s Hill Forts of Rajasthan account emphasizes the relationship between fortifications, inhabited settlements, religious buildings and water infrastructure.
buildings.layout_notes: Gateways and bastions protect an internally occupied hilltop settlement. Palaces, narrow passages, projecting balconies and shrines form a layered architectural landscape.
buildings.date_label: Founded 1156 CE; buildings span later centuries

buildings.name: Mahabodhi Temple
buildings.summary: A tall brick Buddhist temple marking the sacred setting associated with the Buddha’s enlightenment.
buildings.history: The sacred site is associated with the Buddha’s enlightenment and an earlier Ashokan foundation. UNESCO dates the principal surviving brick temple to the fifth or sixth century; that building date is distinct from the age of the religious site.
buildings.layout_notes: A tall tapering sanctuary tower anchors the sacred precinct. Surrounding votive monuments, railings and associated spaces record subsequent devotional activity.
buildings.date_label: Principal surviving temple, 5th–6th centuries CE; earlier sacred site

buildings.name: Nalanda Mahavihara
buildings.summary: An archaeological monastic and scholarly complex whose brick courts, cells, shrines and stupas reveal successive building phases.
buildings.history: Nalanda preserves the remains of a major Buddhist monastic and scholarly institution with a much longer history than any single building. UNESCO describes occupation from the third century BCE to the thirteenth century CE; the surviving architectural phases are a separate question.
buildings.layout_notes: Brick monasteries organize cells around courts. Temples, stupas and successive building levels reveal both institutional planning and later rebuilding.

buildings.name: Charminar
buildings.summary: A four-sided urban monument with monumental arched passages and corner minarets at the heart of historic Hyderabad.
buildings.history: The Hyderabad district account dates the monument to 1591 under Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah. Several explanations for its commemoration survive; the record does not turn an uncertain founding story into an established fact.
buildings.layout_notes: Four large arches define passages through the square structure. Corner minarets, balconies and upper-level spaces mark the monument’s relationship to the surrounding streets.

buildings.name: Basilica of Bom Jesus
buildings.summary: An early modern basilica whose articulated façade and interior preserve important evidence of Portuguese-era religious architecture.
buildings.history: The basilica is a component of Goa’s World Heritage churches and convents and houses the tomb associated with Francis Xavier. Its early modern architecture belongs to the wider exchange of European religious forms in Portuguese Asia.
buildings.layout_notes: An articulated façade uses Classical architectural orders. The longitudinal church interior and associated funerary setting should be distinguished from the larger Old Goa group.

buildings.name: Harmandir Sahib
buildings.summary: A sacred pavilion approached across a causeway within a large pool, with entrances emphasizing access from all directions.
buildings.history: The SGPC account associates planning and construction with successive Sikh Gurus and records the late-sixteenth-century foundation. The temple’s subsequent rebuilding and surface treatment are later phases, not evidence that the visible fabric all dates from the foundation.
buildings.layout_notes: A causeway connects the sacred pavilion with its surrounding precinct across the Amrit Sarovar. Access from four sides and the low setting express the temple’s particular spatial conception.
buildings.date_label: Late 16th–early 17th-century foundation; later rebuilding and gilding

buildings.name: Victoria Memorial
buildings.summary: A marble memorial and museum combining a domed monumental composition with formal gardens and European and Indian design references.
buildings.history: The memorial belongs to the early twentieth century and now functions as a museum. Its monumental composition combines European Classical and Renaissance references with Indian architectural elements; it broadens the archive beyond ancient and medieval monuments.
buildings.layout_notes: A central dome organizes a symmetrical memorial building. Subsidiary domed forms, colonnaded approaches and formal gardens create the larger civic composition.

buildings.name: Shiva Dol
buildings.summary: An Ahom-period Shiva temple beside the Sivasagar tank, distinguished by its rising sanctuary tower.
buildings.history: The Assam district account places the Shivadol, Vishnudol and Devidol beside the tank in 1734 under Queen Madambika. This record concerns the Shiva temple, not every structure at the larger water precinct.
buildings.layout_notes: A rising sanctuary tower gives the temple a strong vertical profile. Its relationship to the tank and adjoining shrines is an important part of the setting.

buildings.name: Martand Sun Temple
buildings.summary: A ruined solar temple whose monumental central shrine and surrounding colonnaded court occupy an elevated Kashmir setting.
buildings.history: The ruined temple is attributed to Lalitaditya Muktapida in the eighth century in the institutional archaeological record. Its surviving architecture should be read as evidence of an incomplete structure rather than an intact reconstructed temple.
buildings.layout_notes: A monumental central shrine stands within a large colonnaded enclosure. Gateways, court space and framed mountain views organize the elevated site.

buildings.name: Sree Padmanabhaswamy Temple
buildings.summary: A living Vishnu temple blending Kerala and Dravidian architectural traditions, with a prominent gateway tower and processional spaces.
buildings.history: The original foundation is not securely dated, as the district account explicitly notes. Later rebuilding and the living ritual tradition produced the present ensemble, which Kerala Tourism describes as a blend of Kerala and Dravidian architecture. Kerala Tourism records renovation in 1733; this is not a founding date.
buildings.layout_notes: The gopuram marks the entrance to the temple precinct. Processional corridors, sculpted surfaces and associated water spaces form part of the broader sacred setting.
